title: Priority decay on stale shard lease causes low-priority requests to become unthrottled
creator: Sofia Chen
description:
Summary: During a geo failover scenario, the shard lease refresher occasionally fails to reconcile priority decay state for per-key accumulators. The system then applies a time-based priority decay that incorrectly elevates the effective allowance for low-priority requests, allowing them to bypass normal throttles for a short window. This results in unmetered or undercounted requests and potential billing exposure.

Technical context: Our rate limiting runtime maintains two orthogonal pieces of state per logical key: (1) a token accumulator (bucket) and (2) a priority score that decays over time for low-priority classes to enable backpressure. Shard leases ensure a single authoritative writer per key. When a shard lease heartbeat is lost and the lease is considered stale, the lease manager triggers a local priority-decay fast-path to avoid stall; however, the fast-path was implemented to mutate the local priority without revalidating the token accumulator epoch. In single-shard normal flows this is safe; during cross-shard geo failovers it permits a period where priority is lowered while the token accumulator snapshot is stale, effectively widening the allowance window for the low-priority class.

Why new and different: Most recent tickets looked at duplicate meter events, shard collisions, or token-bucket desync. This bug is about an ordering problem between priority-decay and accumulator epoch reconciliation that transiently changes throttling semantics (not raw double-counting). It mixes policy evaluation ordering with lease lifecycle, and has both correctness and billing implications.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Deploy a two-region runtime with shard affinity (region-a primary, region-b replica).
2) Configure a per-key policy with a low-priority class that uses time-decay and a small bucket (e.g., 10 tokens, refill 1/sec).
3) Start steady low-priority traffic to consume tokens until near 0 allowance.
4) Simulate a transient network partition causing region-a lease heartbeats to fail and region-b to assume leadership for those keys (fast failover).
5) Observe that for ~10-30s low-priority requests in region-b are admitted despite token counts indicating exhaustion. Check metrics and request traces for bypassed throttles.
observed_behavior: Low-priority requests are accepted for a short window after a shard-leader transition. Request traces show policy evals reporting an elevated priority_score and token_accumulator epoch behind the authoritative store. Billing logs show a burst of unmetered or under-attributed requests to the org over the 10-30s window.
expected_behavior: During lease transitions the runtime should not apply local priority-decay that can widen admission windows unless the token accumulator epoch has been reconciled with the authoritative shard. Either delay priority-decay until reconciliation completes or make the decay decision conservative (no-op) when lease state is stale.
impact_summary: Customer impact: medium-high for orgs with tight per-key quotas and mixed-priority traffic. Risk: financial exposure due to unbilled requests, and potential SLA violations for higher-priority tenants if low-priority traffic preempts capacity. Observed in internal staging with a synthetic load generator and correlated to a small production incident affecting 3 customers for ~12s each.
mitigation: Hotfix: disable local priority-decay fast-path when lease_heartbeat_age > 2s (deployed to regions A/B) — reduces time window for unsafe decay.
Fallback: enforce read-after-write check where policy evals consult epoch tag; if epoch mismatch, apply conservative deny for low-priority class until reconciled.
Monitoring: add an alert on priority_score drift vs token_accumulator_epoch > 0 for any key with > 5 rejected high-priority requests in same window.
proposed_fix: Primary fix: change the lease-manager/priority-decay sequence so that any local priority mutation is gated by a successful epoch reconciliation with the accumulator store. Introduce an atomic update path: fetch epoch -> apply reconcile -> apply decay in single coordinated transition. Add unit tests and chaos test that exercises heartbeat loss + failover.
rollout_plan: 1) Merge runtime PR with gating logic and tests (staging smoke).
2) Canary deploy to 5% traffic in a non-critical region for 24 hours with synthetic low-priority load.
3) If stable, roll to 50% then 100% over next 48 hours.
4) Post-deploy: run mass-scan to compare priority_score vs epoch drift across all keys and validate no residual windows.
notes: Engineering notes: this touches hot path in policy-eval; keep latency overhead <1ms. We should prefer a logical epoch tag compare rather than a blocking read to authoritative store in steady state.

Design trade-offs: conservative approach denies low-priority requests during ambiguity (safer billing) but may increase user-perceived throttling; need product sign-off on acceptable temporary strictness.
PM feedback: customers prefer over-throttling to unexpected free capacity. Suggest customer-facing postmortem and potential billing reconciliation process for affected customers.
qa_steps: Add unit tests for epoch+decay gating logic in rate-evaluator module.
Integration test: simulate lease heartbeat drop and assert low-priority requests are denied until epoch reconcile completes.
Load test: verify no >1% increase in p50/p95 policy-eval latency after change.
updates: 2026-03-06: Initial triage — reproduced in staging with rl-tools harness (Sofia).
2026-03-07: Confirmed billing anomaly correlated to priority_score drift; notified PMs and SRE (Rohit).
2026-03-09: Deployed mitigation (disable fast-path when heartbeat_age>2s) to canary; observed reduction in incident rate (Eleanor verified).
2026-03-11: PR#4218 opened with gating logic; code review started (assign reviewers: @miguel, @eleanor).
2026-03-12: Security and Product reviewed trade-offs; proceeding with canary rollout plan.
